name: Company cases of AI use, with outcomes and sources
description: Named companies that used AI at work, one row per case. Each row gives the company, what it does, the country, the period, the size band, the kind of work AI was used for, how the case turned out, who produced the figures, the practices the case bears on, and the public sources.

rows.title: accessiBe: an AI plug-in sold as making any website accessible, and a $1 million order
rows.summary: accessiBe sold website owners an AI plug-in and said it would make any site meet accessibility standards. The US consumer regulator said it did not, and that reviews praising it were paid for. The company paid $1 million.

rows.title: Air AI: the US regulator says small firms were sold “AI that replaces staff” and lost up to $250,000
rows.summary: Air AI sold small-business owners “conversational AI” that it said could replace customer-service staff, with promises that they would earn their money back. The US consumer regulator alleges that buyers lost up to $250,000 each and that promised refunds were rarely paid. Under a proposed settlement the owners are banned from marketing business opportunities.

rows.title: Bunnings: facial recognition on every shopper in 63 stores, and what the regulator and the tribunal decided

rows.summary: In April 2025 Shopify’s chief executive made AI use a baseline expectation for every employee, and told teams to show why AI could not do the work before asking for more staff. Since then Shopify’s headcount has fallen slightly while revenue rose 30%, and its leaders say AI writes over half its code. They also name what went wrong: a leaderboard of AI use that rewarded the wrong thing, more code than reviewers can keep up with, and AI work passed to colleagues unread. Every figure is the company’s own.

rows.title: Siemens: inspectors caught more defects when the AI showed what it had seen
rows.summary: Researchers gave 48 inspectors at a Siemens electronics factory an AI aid for checking circuit boards. Half saw only the AI’s score. Half also saw a picture marking where the AI had found a problem. The second group caught more defects, and most of them did better than the AI working alone.

rows.title: Temple & Webster: an online furniture retailer with about 200 staff put AI into customer care first
rows.summary: Temple & Webster sells furniture online with about 200 employees. It reports that AI and automation handle 80% of customer contacts in whole or in part, and that customer care now costs over 60% less as a share of revenue. It then set up central approval, training and a contact person for AI in every department.

rows.title: UK Department for Business and Trade: 1,000 Copilot licences, satisfied users, no proven productivity gain
rows.summary: A UK government department gave 1,000 staff an AI assistant inside the office software they already used, and measured the result. Most users were satisfied and writing tasks went faster. Some tasks went slower or came out worse, and the department found no evidence of higher productivity.

rows.title: Workado: an AI detector sold as 98% accurate that tested at 53%
rows.summary: Workado sold a tool that claims to tell AI-written text from human writing, and advertised it as 98% accurate. The US consumer regulator said independent testing put it at 53% on general text. Buyers had only the vendor’s word.

rows.title: WPP: £300 million a year on an AI platform, and revenue still fell
rows.summary: WPP, one of the largest advertising groups, invested heavily in its own AI platform and reported wide use by staff. Its revenue still fell in 2025. Investing in AI did not, on its own, protect an agency’s income.

rows.title: Zillow Offers: home-price forecasts missed, and Zillow shut its home-buying business
rows.summary: Zillow bought homes to resell, at prices set with its own algorithms and in-person checks. In 2021 its forecasts of resale prices missed by far more than it had planned for. It wrote down $407.9 million of homes, shut the business and cut about a quarter of its staff. Zillow named labour and supply problems as well as the forecasts.
